screens.title: Advanced Performance Troubleshooting and Query Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will deepen your ability to find and fix slow database queries. You will learn to read execution plans, use Query Store to review historical behavior and to force stable plans, and to query server-state views and functions for real-time diagnosis. We'll compare equivalent tools for Azure S Q L, PostgreSQL, and MySQL so you can apply the right technique in each environment. You'll also learn practical index strategies for OLTP and OLAP workloads, how to capture granular events with Extended Events, and common traps like parameter sniffing and stale statistics. For example, when a reporting query suddenly regresses after a deployment, Query Store can reveal the prior plan and let you force it so performance stabilizes without code changes. A common misconception is that adding indexes always improves performance; we'll show why writes can slow and how to measure index utility. By the end of this chapter you will be able to locate the expensive operation in a plan, select targeted index changes, gather historical evidence from Query Store, and collect fine-grained events to reproduce intermittent problems. Think about a recent slow query you have seen: what first metric would you capture to begin your investigation?

Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Advanced Performance

Advanced Performance Troubleshooting

Learn to interpret execution plans, capture history with Query Store, query DMVs, and apply index strategies to improve query responsiveness across Azure SQL, PostgreSQL, and MySQL.

In this lesson
Read plans, use Query Store, query DMVs, review indexes, and capture Extended Events.
Coming up
Hands-on steps to enable Query Store, create sample data, and observe plan changes after an index.
Chapter snapshot
Execution plans, Query Store, DMVs/DMFs, index strategy, Extended Events, and common performance issues like parameter sniffing and outdated statistics.
Concept map
Query plans → Query Store → DMVs → Indexes → Events
Execution Plans
Roadmap of operations and costs that the engine uses to run a query.
Query Store
Historical capture of queries, plans, and runtime stats; can force plans.
DMVs / DMFs
Real-time views giving insight into active requests, waits, and index usage.
Explore Key Topics
Execution plans for diagnostics, Query Store for history and forcing plans, DMVs for live state — practical tools you will use each time you troubleshoot.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives will guide your work through the chapter. First, you will deepen your ability to read and interpret query execution plans so you can identify expensive operations like table scans, sorts, and joins that drive cost. That skill matters because the plan tells you the exact sequence the engine follows and which operations dominate time or input and output. Second, you will learn to use Query Store to capture historical query behavior and to force a previously good plan when a regression happens after an update. Practically, this lets you stabilize performance without changing application code. Third, you'll practice querying Dynamic Management Views and Functions to observe active requests, waits, input and output metrics, and index usage in real time, an essential diagnostic step for blocking or resource contention. Finally, you will analyze index strategies for OLTP versus OLAP workloads and use Extended Events for fine-grained captures. Each objective is paired with a small practical milestone so you can verify competency as you work through the lab steps and checkpoints.

Outcomes you can verify

Each objective maps to a concrete verification: captured plan, DMV output, plan change after indexing, and an Extended Events capture.

Verify Query Store
After enabling, run a sample query and confirm it appears in Top Resource Consuming Queries with captured plans.

screens.title: Query Execution Plans — What they show and how to read them
screens.narratorSegment: A query execution plan is a step-by-step blueprint the database engine uses to run your S Q L. It lists operators such as index seek, index scan, nested loop join, merge join, hash join, and sorts, and it attaches cost or runtime measures to each operation. Reading a plan means identifying the operation or subtree with the highest cost or actual runtime and then tracing why that operation is expensive. For example, a clustered index scan over a large orders table often indicates a missing useful index or a non-sargable predicate. In Azure S Q L you can capture actual execution plans in SSMS or Azure Data Studio; in PostgreSQL you use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to run the query and return actual row counts and timings; in MySQL you use EXPLAIN for the plan overview. A concrete example: a query that filters by YEAR(OrderDate) prevents use of a date index because the predicate is non-sargable; the plan will show a scan and a high cost on that step. A common misconception is to focus only on total cost rather than on confusing estimated cost and actual runtime; actual plans reveal runtime discrepancies often caused by outdated statistics or skewed data. When you identify the expensive operator, ask whether an index, a rewrite of the query, or updated statistics will reduce cost. What single operator in your last slow query would you inspect first?

keyIdea.title: Execution plan essentials
keyIdea.text: Find the highest-cost operator, check whether the predicate is sargable, compare estimated versus actual rows, and choose targeted fixes like index creation or predicate rewrite.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Execution Plans
Definition

What an execution plan tells you

A plan shows operators and costs; reading it focuses on which operator uses the most resources and why.

Operators to watch
Index seek, index scan, table scan, joins, sorts — scans on large tables are often the primary concern.
Estimated vs Actual
Compare estimates to actual row counts; large discrepancies point to stale statistics or skewed data.
Sargability
Make predicates sargable so indexes can be used; functions on columns often prevent seeks.
Key Takeaway

Focus on the operator with highest runtime or I/O. Ask: can an index, a rewrite, or updated statistics reduce its cost?

Example
-- Azure SQL: capture actual plan
SET STATISTICS PROFILE ON;
SELECT p.ProductName, c.CategoryName
FROM Production.Products p
JOIN Production.Categories c ON p.CategoryID = c.CategoryID
WHERE p.Price > 50;
SET STATISTICS PROFILE OFF;
Concrete interpretation
  • Look for a table scan node over Production.Products — that hints at a missing index on Price.
  • If actual rows are much higher than estimated rows, update statistics or investigate data skew.
  • If a JOIN shows a nested loop with many executions, consider join order or different join type via indexing or hints.
Common Mistake
Relying on estimated plans alone. Always compare to actual plans or EXPLAIN ANALYZE output where available.

screens.title: Use Query Store to capture history and force plans
screens.narratorSegment: Query Store records queries, execution plans, and runtime statistics over time so you can compare behavior before and after a change. Enabling Query Store is a configuration step on the database and stores plan history without requiring application changes. Once enabled, you can open Top Resource Consuming Queries and identify queries whose runtime increased after a deployment. The key troubleshooting flow is: identify the query id, review its plan history, choose the previously known good plan, and force it. For example, enabling Query Store with sensible cleanup and size settings captures enough history to compare multiple windows. A hands-on caution: forcing a plan is a mitigation, not a permanent fix — if data distribution changes the forced plan may become suboptimal. A concrete T-S Q L example from the lab shows how to alter database settings to turn Query Store on. After running a slow sample query and inspecting Query Store, you can create an index and watch the plan change from a clustered index scan to an index seek. If that change is temporary or a regression returns, forcing the prior plan gives you an immediate rollback of behavior without changing application code. After forcing, monitor to ensure the forced plan remains effective over time.

keyIdea.title: Query Store workflow
keyIdea.text: Enable Query Store, capture query history, compare plan versions, and force a prior plan to quickly mitigate regressions while monitoring impact.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Query Store
Enable & Configure
Use a balanced set of settings so the store captures useful history without using excessive storage.
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET QUERY_STORE = ON (
  OPERATION_MODE = READ_WRITE,
  CLEANUP_POLICY = (STALE_QUERY_THRESHOLD_DAYS = 30),
  DATA_FLUSH_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 900,
  MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB = 1000,
  INTERVAL_LENGTH_MINUTES = 60,
  SIZE_BASED_CLEANUP_MODE = AUTO,
  QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO
);
Troubleshooting steps
  • Run the target query and find it in Top Resource Consuming Queries.
  • Compare plan versions to find when the regression started.
  • Choose the prior good plan and use the force plan action.
Practical note
Forcing a plan stabilizes performance quickly, but you must monitor data distribution and re-evaluate the forced plan periodically.
Example: observe plan change
-- Create a sample table and run a slow query, then create index
CREATE TABLE dbo.Orders (
  OrderID INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
  CustomerID INT NOT NULL,
  OrderDate DATETIME NOT NULL,
  OrderTotal DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  OrderStatus VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
);
-- Insert many rows (lab step)
SELECT * FROM dbo.Orders WHERE CustomerID = 5000 AND OrderStatus = 'Pending';
-- Optional index
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_CustomerID_OrderStatus ON dbo.Orders (CustomerID, OrderStatus);
What you will see in Query Store
  • A record of the query text and captured plans over time.
  • A plan showing clustered index scan before the index and an index seek after the index is created.
  • Runtime statistics showing improvements in CPU and duration.

screens.title: Use DMVs and DMFs for live performance insight
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic Management Views and Functions offer a window into the engine's current state. They let you list active requests, sessions, input and output statistics, waits, and index usage without changing application code. In Azure S Q L, examples include sys. dm_exec_requests to see currently running requests, sys. dm_exec_sessions for session context, sys. dm_io_virtual_file_stats for input and output activity, and sys. dm_db_index_usage_stats to show index seeks and scans. For PostgreSQL you would use pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_statements, and pg_locks to find active queries, statement aggregates, and lock waits. MySQL exposes similar information through performance_schema and information_schema views. A practical flow for diagnosis is: first use a DMV to identify active long-running requests, then capture the session's query text and plan, then inspect waits and resource counters to determine whether the bottleneck is C P U, input and output, or blocking. For instance, if sys. dm_exec_requests shows a blocking_session_id, you will need to identify the blocker and evaluate whether a transaction is holding locks too long. A common misconception is to assume DMVs are a full historical log; they are current state or aggregated counters and should be sampled or paired with Query Store for history. When you run DMVs regularly you can detect trends and catch intermittent contention early.

keyIdea.text: Query DMVs to find active slow requests, check waits and I/O, and combine with Query Store for historical context when needed.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › DMVs & DMFs
Common DMVs
  • sys.dm_exec_requests — currently executing requests and duration.
  • sys.dm_exec_sessions — session metadata and client info.
  • sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats — seeks, scans, lookups, and updates per index.
  • sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats — file-level I/O counters.
-- Example: active queries in PostgreSQL
SELECT pid, usename, application_name, client_addr, backend_start, state, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active'
ORDER BY query_start;
Investigation flow
  1. Identify long-running or blocked sessions with DMVs.
  2. Capture the query text and execution plan for the session.
  3. Check waits, CPU, and I/O to classify the bottleneck.
  4. Apply fixes: index, query rewrite, statistics update, or transaction tuning.
Key Takeaway
DMVs are best used for immediate diagnosis and when paired with plan captures or Query Store for historical context.

screens.title: Monitoring equivalence: Azure SQL, PostgreSQL, MySQL
screens.narratorSegment: When you move across platforms it's important to know the equivalent tools so you can apply the same investigative pattern. In Azure S Q L the Query Store and DMVs like sys. dm_exec_requests and sys. dm_db_index_usage_stats are central. PostgreSQL offers EXPLAIN ANALYZE for actual plans and views like pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_statements for active and aggregated metrics. MySQL uses EXPLAIN for plan insight and exposes performance_schema and information_schema for runtime metrics. A practical comparison: to see actual runtime statistics for a single query use EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL, while in Azure S Q L you enable actual execution plans in SSMS and can use SET STATISTICS PROFILE ON to capture them; in MySQL you run EXPLAIN and compare the access type and rows estimates. For top resource-consuming queries across time, Query Store in Azure S Q L is the built-in historical store; PostgreSQL may use pg_stat_statements to aggregate statement metrics, and MySQL can use performance_schema aggregated counters. A common mistake is to attempt to force a plan in platforms that don't have an equivalent to Query Store; forcing is an Azure S Q L Query Store feature, so on other platforms you must use hints or plan guides, or tune the query and indexes. Always use the platform-specific view that provides actual runtimes when possible.

keyIdea.title: Platform mapping
keyIdea.text: Azure SQL: Query Store + DMVs; PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN ANALYZE + pg_stat views; MySQL: EXPLAIN + performance_schema — use equivalents to follow the same diagnostic flow.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Platform Comparison
Azure SQL
Query Store for history, DMVs like sys.dm_exec_requests for live state, and Extended Events for granular capture.
SELECT TOP 10 qt.query_sql_text, q.query_id, SUM(rs.avg_cpu_time) AS avg_cpu_time
FROM sys.query_store_query_text qt
JOIN sys.query_store_query q ON qt.query_text_id = q.query_text_id
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p ON q.query_id = p.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs ON p.plan_id = rs.plan_id
GROUP BY qt.query_sql_text, q.query_id
ORDER BY avg_cpu_time DESC;
PostgreSQL
EXPLAIN ANALYZE for actual plans and pg_stat_activity/pg_stat_statements for active and aggregated metrics.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT product_name, price FROM products WHERE price > 100;

SELECT pid, usename, application_name, client_addr, state, query
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active';
MySQL
EXPLAIN for access plan guidance and performance_schema for runtime counters and aggregated metrics.
EXPLAIN SELECT product_name, price FROM products WHERE price > 100;
-- Use performance_schema tables for counters
Tip
Apply the same investigative pattern across platforms: capture current state, capture plan, compare history, apply targeted fixes.

screens.title: Index strategy for OLTP vs OLAP
screens.narratorSegment: Index strategy is not one-size-fits-all. OLTP workloads require highly selective, narrow indexes on columns used in frequent WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, and ORDER BYs so short, efficient seeks are possible for many small transactions. Over-indexing in OLTP hurts write performance because each insert, update, or delete must maintain more index structures. OLAP workloads, by contrast, often benefit from wide indexes and columnstore indexes because queries scan large ranges and aggregate; a columnstore can dramatically reduce input and output for analytical queries over large datasets. Regularly review index usage statistics, for example sys. dm_db_index_usage_stats in Azure S Q L, to find unused indexes that cost nothing for reads but add write overhead. A concrete example: an order-processing OLTP table might have nonclustered indexes on CustomerID and OrderDate for common point lookups, while a sales reporting workload might use a columnstore on date, product, and sales amount for fast aggregates. A common misconception is that more indexes always speed reads; measure index seeks versus index scans and the cost of maintaining indexes on writes. The right strategy balances read patterns, write throughput, and storage; start by measuring index utilization and then add or remove indexes in a test environment before rolling out to production.

keyIdea.title: Index trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Choose selective, narrow indexes for OLTP; prefer columnstore or wider indexes for OLAP. Measure usage to avoid over-indexing that slows writes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Index Strategy
OLTP index rules
  • Use narrow, selective nonclustered indexes on predicate and join columns.
  • Avoid many overlapping indexes that increase write cost.
  • Measure seek vs scan counts and remove unused indexes.
Example
Create a nonclustered index on CustomerID and OrderStatus to support frequent lookups by customer and status.
OLAP index rules
  • Prefer columnstore indexes for large analytic scans and aggregates.
  • Allow wider composite indexes to cover reporting queries.
  • Keep maintenance windows for bulk load and index rebuilds.
Key Takeaway
Pick indexes based on workload access patterns, measure usage, and always validate changes in non-production before production rollout.
Measure
Use sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats to find seeks, scans, and updates per index.
Test
Apply index changes in a staging environment with realistic data volumes before production.
Balance
Weigh read improvements against write overhead and storage impact.

screens.title: Extended Events for targeted, low-overhead captures
screens.narratorSegment: Extended Events are a lightweight mechanism to collect detailed runtime information that helps reproduce intermittent or rare performance problems. Unlike heavy tracing, Extended Events allow you to target specific events such as long-running queries, deadlocks, or particular wait types with minimal performance impact. The typical approach is to define a session with filters for duration or specific query text, collect the event payload to a ring buffer or file, and analyze the captured events offline to see exact parameter values, stack trace context, or locking details. In Azure S Q L you can create an Extended Events session that captures long duration queries and include actions like sql_text and transaction_id in the payload. A concrete scenario: capture events where duration exceeds a threshold, then correlate those events with Query Store entries or DMV snapshots to understand whether a spike was caused by a query plan change, blocking, or input and output saturation. A common misconception is that Extended Events are only for experts; with sensible templates you can start by capturing a few event types and examine the results in Azure Data Studio or SSMS. Always run captures in a controlled manner, export results for analysis, and avoid capturing unnecessarily large payloads in production without retention and storage controls.

Always run captures in a controlled manner, export results for analysis, and avoid capturing unnecessarily large payloads in production without retention and storage controls.

keyIdea.title: Event capture strategy
keyIdea.text: Target specific events with filters, collect minimal payloads, and correlate captures with Query Store and DMVs to diagnose intermittent issues.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Extended Events
Why use Extended Events
Capture detailed, targeted information with low overhead to diagnose intermittent and complex performance issues like deadlocks or long-running statements.
Configuration points
  • Filter by duration, database, or sql_text to reduce noise.
  • Collect only necessary actions like sql_text and transaction_id.
  • Store to file or ring buffer and analyze outside of peak hours.
Example capture
-- Pseudo: create a session to capture long-running queries
-- Define event: sql_statement_completed
-- Filter: duration >= 1000 ms
-- Actions: sql_text, client_app_name, transaction_id
-- Target: event_file or ring_buffer
Analysis tips
  • Correlate event times with Query Store plan changes and DMV snapshots.
  • Search payload for parameter values that reveal skew or pathologic inputs.
  • Use captured transaction_id to link to blocking queries or deadlocks.

screens.title: Common query performance issues and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring root causes that explain most query slowness. Missing or inefficient indexes cause full table scans, increasing input and output and C P U. Poorly written queries — for example, using SELECT * or non-sargable predicates like YEAR(OrderDate) = 2023 — prevent index seeks. Blocking occurs when one session holds locks that prevent others from progressing, which you can detect with DMVs showing blocking_session_id. Outdated statistics make the optimizer choose suboptimal plans because estimated cardinalities are wrong; regular statistics updates help. Parameter sniffing is a subtle cause: when the optimizer compiles a plan based on the first execution's parameters it may not be optimal for other parameter values, producing a plan that performs poorly for typical inputs. For each issue there is a targeted cure: create the right index or add covering columns for missing indexes, rewrite predicates to be sargable, identify and remediate long transactions or use lock escalation controls for blocking, update statistics or use filtered statistics for skewed distributions, and mitigate parameter sniffing by using option(recompile), plan guides, or forced plans carefully after testing. A common error is to apply global fixes like rebuilding all indexes before identifying the actual problem; efficient troubleshooting targets the smallest change that resolves the costly operator you found in the plan.

keyIdea.title: Root causes and remedies
keyIdea.text: Diagnose missing indexes, non-sargable predicates, blocking, outdated statistics, and parameter sniffing. Apply the smallest, measured fix and validate in staging.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Common Issues

Problems

  • Missing indexes: leads to scans and high I/O.
  • Non-sargable predicates: functions on columns prevent seeks.
  • Blocking: long transactions holding locks stop concurrency.
  • Outdated statistics: optimizer misestimates cardinality.
  • Parameter sniffing: a plan optimized for one parameter may be poor for others.

Fixes

  • Create targeted nonclustered or columnstore indexes; evaluate effect on writes.
  • Rewrite predicates to be sargable (avoid wrapping columns in functions).
  • Find blockers via DMVs and reduce transaction scope to lower lock time.
  • Update statistics or use filtered/column-specific statistics for skewed data.
  • Mitigate parameter sniffing with recompile options or by testing forced plans in Query Store.
Pro Tip
Make one change at a time and measure its impact with Query Store or repeatable DMV sampling.
Check your understanding
If a query started doing table scans after a deployment, what two pieces of evidence would you collect first to decide whether to force a plan?

screens.title: Lab: enable Query Store, create data, and observe plan changes
screens.narratorSegment: This guided lab shows the practical verification steps. First, enable Query Store on your test database with sensible parameters so history is kept. Next, create a sample Orders table and populate it with many rows so that queries have measurable runtime. Run a deliberately unindexed query against CustomerID and OrderStatus to provoke a clustered index scan. Use Query Store's Top Resource Consuming Queries to find that query and open its plan history. Then create a nonclustered index on (CustomerID, OrderStatus), rerun the query, and observe several changes: the plan should move from a scan to an index seek, and runtime statistics in Query Store should improve. If the plan does not change, check whether the predicate is sargable and whether statistics require updating. A common misconception is to expect immediate improvement after index creation; sometimes you must clear the plan cache or rerun with new parameter values to compile a new plan. Finally, if you observe a prior good plan in Query Store, try the force plan action to validate that forcing returns the expected performance. This lab reinforces measuring before and after, validating changes in a non-production environment, and verifying improvements with recorded evidence.

keyIdea.title: Lab verification
keyIdea.text: Enable Query Store, run a slow query, create a targeted index, and confirm plan and runtime improvements before applying to production.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Hands-on Lab
Starter T-SQL (lab)
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET QUERY_STORE = ON (
  OPERATION_MODE = READ_WRITE,
  CLEANUP_POLICY = (STALE_QUERY_THRESHOLD_DAYS = 30),
  MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB = 1000,
  QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO
);

CREATE TABLE dbo.Orders (
  OrderID INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
  CustomerID INT NOT NULL,
  OrderDate DATETIME NOT NULL,
  OrderTotal DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  OrderStatus VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
);
-- Insert many rows (use loop or bulk load for lab)
SELECT * FROM dbo.Orders WHERE CustomerID = 5000 AND OrderStatus = 'Pending';

CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_CustomerID_OrderStatus ON dbo.Orders (CustomerID, OrderStatus);
Verification steps
  1. Run the unindexed query and record runtime in Query Store.
  2. Create the nonclustered index and rerun the query.
  3. Open plan history in Query Store and compare plans (scan → seek) and runtime stats.
  4. If regression exists, consider forcing prior plan or checking stats and parameter values.
Key Takeaway
Measure before and after. Use Query Store as the evidence repository for your change and rollback decisions.

screens.title: Assessing regressions and the force plan decision
screens.narratorSegment: Forcing a plan is a powerful quick-mitigation but should be used thoughtfully. Use Query Store to compare the historical plans and their runtime metrics. If a query regressed after a change and a previously captured plan consistently performed better, forcing that good plan can restore performance without changing application code. The decision process should include: evidence that the prior plan runs faster across representative parameters, validation that the forced plan will not break correctness, and a plan for monitoring the forced plan's effectiveness over time. Always test forcing in a staging environment to observe any unintended side effects. Be aware that data distribution can change, and a forced plan that was good yesterday may be suboptimal later; schedule periodic re-evaluation. A common misconception is that forcing eliminates the need to find the root cause — forcing stabilizes performance fast, but you still should investigate why the regression occurred, whether it's outdated statistics, parameter sniffing, or schema changes. After forcing, use Query Store metrics to check C P U, duration, and logical reads and set alerts if those metrics worsen. Finally, document the reason for forcing and the planned rollback or re-evaluation date so the operation stays visible to the team.

keyIdea.text: Force plans as an emergency mitigation after testing and with monitoring and re-evaluation plans to avoid long-term suboptimal execution.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Force Plan Decision
Decision checklist
  • Evidence: prior plan shows better timings across representative parameters.
  • Correctness: forced plan must return correct results for all inputs.
  • Test: validate in staging under similar data volumes.
  • Monitor: set alerts on duration and CPU after forcing.
Governance
Record the reason for forcing, expected benefit, and a re-evaluation date. Forcing is a mitigation, not a root-cause fix.
Common Mistake
Leaving forced plans indefinitely without monitoring or revisiting when data distribution shifts.
Check your understanding
If a forced plan stops matching data distribution, what monitoring signals should alert you to remove or re-evaluate the forced plan?

screens.title: Measurement and change management for performance tuning
screens.narratorSegment: Any change to indexes, plans, or capture settings must follow measurement and change-management practices. Start by collecting baseline metrics: duration, C P U, logical reads, and plan identifiers from Query Store or sampled DMV snapshots. Apply changes in a staging environment with realistic data volume and workload. After a controlled change, rerun the same queries and compare Query Store entries or DMV samples to measure improvements. Use performance counters like logical reads to confirm input and output reductions and ensure that write throughput is not negatively affected by added indexes. When rolling out to production, choose maintenance windows for index builds, and use phased rollouts where possible. If you force a plan, pair it with a rollback plan and scheduled re-evaluation. Keep a short runbook that lists the steps, verification queries, and alert thresholds so other team members can validate or revert changes. A common pitfall is rolling index changes directly into production without a reproducible verification script. Instead, create a small set of queries that prove the issue and the fix; run them before and after, and store the results as evidence. This practice reduces risk and ensures you can explain the change if production behaves differently than expected.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Change Management
Baseline
Capture duration, CPU, logical reads, and plan IDs before any change. Store these values as your control set.
Staging
Reproduce workload at realistic scale and test index or query changes. Validate plans and metrics here first.
Rollout
Use phased rollout, maintenance windows, and a rollback plan. Monitor Query Store or DMVs for regressions after change.
Repeatable tests
Keep a small suite of queries to run before and after changes; record the results for traceability.
Runbook
Document steps, verification queries, alert thresholds, and rollback steps so others can validate or revert the change.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These key concepts are the anchors for troubleshooting and tuning. First, a Query Execution Plan is the engine's roadmap; find the expensive operator and decide whether an index, rewrite, or statistics update is the right fix. Second, Query Store is your historical evidence repository in Azure S Q L — use it to compare plan versions and force prior good plans as a mitigation. Third, DMVs and DMFs provide live state for active sessions, waits, and index usage — sample them regularly to find blocking or resource contention. Fourth, index strategy differs between OLTP and OLAP; prefer selective, narrow indexes for transactional systems and columnstore or wide indexes for analytics. Fifth, Extended Events give targeted, low-overhead captures for intermittent problems like long-running queries or deadlocks. Finally, measure, test in staging, and govern any change with runbooks and rollback plans. Keep these concepts in mind as you practice the lab steps and interpret the Query Store and DMV outputs.

Query Execution Plan
Shows steps and costs; use actual plans to compare estimated and real work.
Query Store
Historical capture of queries and plans; useful for identifying regressions and forcing plans.

Provide live state: active sessions, waits, I/O stats, and index usage for immediate diagnosis.
Remember to test changes in non-production, measure before and after, and avoid permanent fixes without evidence. Use Query Store as your evidence store and Extended Events for fine-grained captures.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference

Together these patterns let you find the cause, validate a fix in staging, and roll out changes safely with measurable evidence. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will deepen your ability to find and fix slow database queries. You will learn to read execution plans, use Query Store to review historical behavior and to force stable plans, and to query server-state views and functions for real-time diagnosis. We'll compare equivalent tools for Azure S Q L, PostgreSQL, and MySQL so you can apply the right technique in each environment. You'll also learn practical index strategies for OLTP and OLAP workloads, how to capture granular events with Extended Events, and common traps like parameter sniffing and stale statistics. For example, when a reporting query suddenly regresses after a deployment, Query Store can reveal the prior plan and let you force it so performance stabilizes without code changes. A common misconception is that adding indexes always improves performance; we'll show why writes can slow and how to measure index utility. By the end of this chapter you will be able to locate the expensive operation in a plan, select targeted index changes, gather historical evidence from Query Store, and collect fine-grained events to reproduce intermittent problems. Think about a recent slow query you have seen: what first metric would you capture to begin your investigation?

These objectives will guide your work through the chapter. First, you will deepen your ability to read and interpret query execution plans so you can identify expensive operations like table scans, sorts, and joins that drive cost. That skill matters because the plan tells you the exact sequence the engine follows and which operations dominate time or input and output. Second, you will learn to use Query Store to capture historical query behavior and to force a previously good plan when a regression happens after an update. Practically, this lets you stabilize performance without changing application code. Third, you'll practice querying Dynamic Management Views and Functions to observe active requests, waits, input and output metrics, and index usage in real time, an essential diagnostic step for blocking or resource contention. Finally, you will analyze index strategies for OLTP versus OLAP workloads and use Extended Events for fine-grained captures. Each objective is paired with a small practical milestone so you can verify competency as you work through the lab steps and checkpoints.

This second objectives slide ties each learning goal to a practical outcome. You will enable Query Store and confirm it captures query text and plans; you'll run a slow query and use the store to find its top-consuming entry. You will write DMV queries to list active sessions, examine input and output statistics, and check index usage. You will design and test a nonclustered index for a slow predicate and measure whether the plan changes from a scan to an index seek, demonstrating measurable improvement. You will configure an Extended Events session to capture long-running queries or deadlocks, then review the collected events to diagnose intermittent issues. Each outcome includes a lightweight verification step so you can prove competency: a captured plan in Query Store, a DMV result showing active waits, a visible change from scan to seek in the execution plan, and an event capture containing the target query. Together these steps move you from theory to repeatable troubleshooting practice.

A query execution plan is a step-by-step blueprint the database engine uses to run your S Q L. It lists operators such as index seek, index scan, nested loop join, merge join, hash join, and sorts, and it attaches cost or runtime measures to each operation. Reading a plan means identifying the operation or subtree with the highest cost or actual runtime and then tracing why that operation is expensive. For example, a clustered index scan over a large orders table often indicates a missing useful index or a non-sargable predicate. In Azure S Q L you can capture actual execution plans in SSMS or Azure Data Studio; in PostgreSQL you use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to run the query and return actual row counts and timings; in MySQL you use EXPLAIN for the plan overview. A concrete example: a query that filters by YEAR(OrderDate) prevents use of a date index because the predicate is non-sargable; the plan will show a scan and a high cost on that step. A common misconception is to focus only on total cost rather than on confusing estimated cost and actual runtime; actual plans reveal runtime discrepancies often caused by outdated statistics or skewed data. When you identify the expensive operator, ask whether an index, a rewrite of the query, or updated statistics will reduce cost. What single operator in your last slow query would you inspect first?

Query Store records queries, execution plans, and runtime statistics over time so you can compare behavior before and after a change. Enabling Query Store is a configuration step on the database and stores plan history without requiring application changes. Once enabled, you can open Top Resource Consuming Queries and identify queries whose runtime increased after a deployment. The key troubleshooting flow is: identify the query id, review its plan history, choose the previously known good plan, and force it. For example, enabling Query Store with sensible cleanup and size settings captures enough history to compare multiple windows. A hands-on caution: forcing a plan is a mitigation, not a permanent fix — if data distribution changes the forced plan may become suboptimal. A concrete T-S Q L example from the lab shows how to alter database settings to turn Query Store on. After running a slow sample query and inspecting Query Store, you can create an index and watch the plan change from a clustered index scan to an index seek. If that change is temporary or a regression returns, forcing the prior plan gives you an immediate rollback of behavior without changing application code. After forcing, monitor to ensure the forced plan remains effective over time.

Dynamic Management Views and Functions offer a window into the engine's current state. They let you list active requests, sessions, input and output statistics, waits, and index usage without changing application code. In Azure S Q L, examples include sys. dm_exec_requests to see currently running requests, sys. dm_exec_sessions for session context, sys. dm_io_virtual_file_stats for input and output activity, and sys. dm_db_index_usage_stats to show index seeks and scans. For PostgreSQL you would use pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_statements, and pg_locks to find active queries, statement aggregates, and lock waits. MySQL exposes similar information through performance_schema and information_schema views. A practical flow for diagnosis is: first use a DMV to identify active long-running requests, then capture the session's query text and plan, then inspect waits and resource counters to determine whether the bottleneck is C P U, input and output, or blocking. For instance, if sys. dm_exec_requests shows a blocking_session_id, you will need to identify the blocker and evaluate whether a transaction is holding locks too long. A common misconception is to assume DMVs are a full historical log; they are current state or aggregated counters and should be sampled or paired with Query Store for history. When you run DMVs regularly you can detect trends and catch intermittent contention early.

When you move across platforms it's important to know the equivalent tools so you can apply the same investigative pattern. In Azure S Q L the Query Store and DMVs like sys. dm_exec_requests and sys. dm_db_index_usage_stats are central. PostgreSQL offers EXPLAIN ANALYZE for actual plans and views like pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_statements for active and aggregated metrics. MySQL uses EXPLAIN for plan insight and exposes performance_schema and information_schema for runtime metrics. A practical comparison: to see actual runtime statistics for a single query use EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL, while in Azure S Q L you enable actual execution plans in SSMS and can use SET STATISTICS PROFILE ON to capture them; in MySQL you run EXPLAIN and compare the access type and rows estimates. For top resource-consuming queries across time, Query Store in Azure S Q L is the built-in historical store; PostgreSQL may use pg_stat_statements to aggregate statement metrics, and MySQL can use performance_schema aggregated counters. A common mistake is to attempt to force a plan in platforms that don't have an equivalent to Query Store; forcing is an Azure S Q L Query Store feature, so on other platforms you must use hints or plan guides, or tune the query and indexes. Always use the platform-specific view that provides actual runtimes when possible.

Index strategy is not one-size-fits-all. OLTP workloads require highly selective, narrow indexes on columns used in frequent WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, and ORDER BYs so short, efficient seeks are possible for many small transactions. Over-indexing in OLTP hurts write performance because each insert, update, or delete must maintain more index structures. OLAP workloads, by contrast, often benefit from wide indexes and columnstore indexes because queries scan large ranges and aggregate; a columnstore can dramatically reduce input and output for analytical queries over large datasets. Regularly review index usage statistics, for example sys. dm_db_index_usage_stats in Azure S Q L, to find unused indexes that cost nothing for reads but add write overhead. A concrete example: an order-processing OLTP table might have nonclustered indexes on CustomerID and OrderDate for common point lookups, while a sales reporting workload might use a columnstore on date, product, and sales amount for fast aggregates. A common misconception is that more indexes always speed reads; measure index seeks versus index scans and the cost of maintaining indexes on writes. The right strategy balances read patterns, write throughput, and storage; start by measuring index utilization and then add or remove indexes in a test environment before rolling out to production.

Extended Events are a lightweight mechanism to collect detailed runtime information that helps reproduce intermittent or rare performance problems. Unlike heavy tracing, Extended Events allow you to target specific events such as long-running queries, deadlocks, or particular wait types with minimal performance impact. The typical approach is to define a session with filters for duration or specific query text, collect the event payload to a ring buffer or file, and analyze the captured events offline to see exact parameter values, stack trace context, or locking details. In Azure S Q L you can create an Extended Events session that captures long duration queries and include actions like sql_text and transaction_id in the payload. A concrete scenario: capture events where duration exceeds a threshold, then correlate those events with Query Store entries or DMV snapshots to understand whether a spike was caused by a query plan change, blocking, or input and output saturation. A common misconception is that Extended Events are only for experts; with sensible templates you can start by capturing a few event types and examine the results in Azure Data Studio or SSMS. Always run captures in a controlled manner, export results for analysis, and avoid capturing unnecessarily large payloads in production without retention and storage controls.

Poorly written queries — for example, using SELECT * or non-sargable predicates like YEAR(OrderDate) = 2023 — prevent index seeks. Blocking occurs when one session holds locks that prevent others from progressing, which you can detect with DMVs showing blocking_session_id. Parameter sniffing is a subtle cause: when the optimizer compiles a plan based on the first execution's parameters it may not be optimal for other parameter values, producing a plan that performs poorly for typical inputs. A common error is to apply global fixes like rebuilding all indexes before identifying the actual problem; efficient troubleshooting targets the smallest change that resolves the costly operator you found in the plan.

Finally, if you observe a prior good plan in Query Store, try the force plan action to validate that forcing returns the expected performance. This lab reinforces measuring before and after, validating changes in a non-production environment, and verifying improvements with recorded evidence.

Forcing a plan is a powerful quick-mitigation but should be used thoughtfully. Use Query Store to compare the historical plans and their runtime metrics. If a query regressed after a change and a previously captured plan consistently performed better, forcing that good plan can restore performance without changing application code. The decision process should include: evidence that the prior plan runs faster across representative parameters, validation that the forced plan will not break correctness, and a plan for monitoring the forced plan's effectiveness over time. Always test forcing in a staging environment to observe any unintended side effects. Be aware that data distribution can change, and a forced plan that was good yesterday may be suboptimal later; schedule periodic re-evaluation. A common misconception is that forcing eliminates the need to find the root cause — forcing stabilizes performance fast, but you still should investigate why the regression occurred, whether it's outdated statistics, parameter sniffing, or schema changes. After forcing, use Query Store metrics to check C P U, duration, and logical reads and set alerts if those metrics worsen. Finally, document the reason for forcing and the planned rollback or re-evaluation date so the operation stays visible to the team.

Any change to indexes, plans, or capture settings must follow measurement and change-management practices. Start by collecting baseline metrics: duration, C P U, logical reads, and plan identifiers from Query Store or sampled DMV snapshots. Apply changes in a staging environment with realistic data volume and workload. After a controlled change, rerun the same queries and compare Query Store entries or DMV samples to measure improvements. Use performance counters like logical reads to confirm input and output reductions and ensure that write throughput is not negatively affected by added indexes. When rolling out to production, choose maintenance windows for index builds, and use phased rollouts where possible. If you force a plan, pair it with a rollback plan and scheduled re-evaluation. Keep a short runbook that lists the steps, verification queries, and alert thresholds so other team members can validate or revert changes. A common pitfall is rolling index changes directly into production without a reproducible verification script. Instead, create a small set of queries that prove the issue and the fix; run them before and after, and store the results as evidence. This practice reduces risk and ensures you can explain the change if production behaves differently than expected.

These key concepts are the anchors for troubleshooting and tuning. First, a Query Execution Plan is the engine's roadmap; find the expensive operator and decide whether an index, rewrite, or statistics update is the right fix. Second, Query Store is your historical evidence repository in Azure S Q L — use it to compare plan versions and force prior good plans as a mitigation. Third, DMVs and DMFs provide live state for active sessions, waits, and index usage — sample them regularly to find blocking or resource contention. Fourth, index strategy differs between OLTP and OLAP; prefer selective, narrow indexes for transactional systems and columnstore or wide indexes for analytics. Fifth, Extended Events give targeted, low-overhead captures for intermittent problems like long-running queries or deadlocks. Finally, measure, test in staging, and govern any change with runbooks and rollback plans. Keep these concepts in mind as you practice the lab steps and interpret the Query Store and DMV outputs.

Keep these three quick reminders handy. First, always identify the single expensive operator in a plan and target the smallest change that removes that expense. Second, use Query Store to gather historical evidence and to force plans only after testing, with monitoring and a re-evaluation plan. Third, use DMVs for live troubleshooting and Extended Events for low-overhead, targeted captures of intermittent problems. Together these patterns let you find the cause, validate a fix in staging, and roll out changes safely with measurable evidence. Carry a short checklist with the queries you use to collect baseline metrics, the verification queries you will run after a change, and the rollback steps so your tuning work is repeatable and auditable.
